newsitem.title: INDIA: India says market can set rupee rate, within limits.
newsitem.headline: India says market can set rupee rate, within limits.

text.p: Judging by Indian monetary authorities' words and action currency traders can play with the rupee anywhere between 35.75-90 per dollar, albeit under the watchful eye of the central bank, dealers said on Monday.
The Reserve Bank of India has intervened on a daily basis within that range, but as soon as the 35.75 level is neared the central bank dollar buying become heavier, they said.
Both the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor Chakaravaty Rangarajan and Finance Minister Palaniappen Chidambaram have said the market should set the exchange rate.
But only regular central bank intervention has stopped the rupee firming sharply. Chidambaram spelt out the RBI strategy in an interview with Reuters Financial Television on Sunday.
"The RBI is not intervening indiscriminately," the Finance Minister said. "Within a band it allows the rupee to fluctuate and it's only when it goes beyond the band does the RBI intervene."
The RBI's recent forays into the market have signalled how far the market can go.

"I think a 35.75-35.90 range seems to be indicated if you look at the two levels of intervention," said a dealer. "They (RBI) stepped in when the rupee looked like breaking 35.75 but allowed the market to find its own level back from 35.89."
In late trade Monday, the rupee was quoted 35.835/842, against 35.840/845 at Friday's close.
RBI intervention is one-way at the moment. Poor dollar demand and strong supply will keep the rupee buoyant in the near term and only the RBI can stem its rise, dealers said.
"At the moment the only demand is from the RBI," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "Left to itself, the rupee can only appreciate."
Dealers also said the situation was ideal for building up foreign exchange reserves, currently equivalent to seven months imports at $26.65 billion, ahead of an end goal of full convertibility.
Exporters have been asking for a depreciation in the rupee against the dollar, complaining that its strength is undermining their competitiveness.
Analysts also reckoned that the rupee should depreciate by anywhere between three and six percent annually to reflect inflation and other economic fundamentals.
But Chidambaram said on Sunday the rupee was currently at the right level and the market should set the rate.
"No, I do not think we should induce a depreciation just to boost someone's confidence," Chidambaram said in reply to a question whether the rupee should be weakened.
"Once you say the rupee will find its level in the market, then you must leave it to the market," he said.
The rupee has traded in a broad 35.75-35.90 per dollar range since last July. In recent weeks it has threatened to break through the 35.75 barrier but was blocked by RBI intervention.

Dealers said the RBI bought $400-500 million last week to push the rupee down to its current levels from last Monday's opening of 35.75. RBI purchases weakened the rupee to 35.89 on Wednesday before it rallied to current levels.
